Or thirdly, Actions which in themselves are of indifferent Nature, neither commanded nor forbiden in the Word. Our taking one part in these Actions, rather then another, may be a <ns0:hi>Scandal,</ns0:hi> that is an <ns0:hi>Offence.</ns0:hi> What our Saviour here saith, is certainly true, concerning all these kinds of Offences, considering the Complexion of the World, and the Corruption which is Mens hearts. It is impossible but that Offences will come. But I must confess that I incline to think, that the <ns0:hi>Offences</ns0:hi> primarily intended by our Saviour here, are those of the first sort, and that by them are meant <ns0:hi>Persecutions of the People of God.</ns0:hi> To the Authors of which our Saviour denounceth Woe. So that our Saviour by this, lets the World know, the special pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tection under which he hath taken his People, so as tho he knew there would arise those, who would <ns0:hi>hurt</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>destroy</ns0:hi> in his holy Mountain; yet he declares, that they shall not go unpunished, but they had better dye the most certain Death imaginable, (such must b<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> the Death of him who is thrown into the Sea, with a Milstone a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bout his Neck) than to that degree expose himself to the Ven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />geance of God, a guilt of that Nature, that there is not much more hope for him to escape Gods Vengeance, than there would be of a Man escaping with his Life, whom we should see thrown into the Sea, with a Milstone appendant to him. I do very well know that it is also highly dangerous, to tempt or sollicite a Child of God to Sin, either by our Words or Action; but I do not think it the design of our Lord in this place, so much to express that as the other.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Take heed to your selves: If thy brother tres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pass against thee, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 17.12. James 5.19.</ns0:note> rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 And if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> hath something of the same tendency in, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 18.21. mentioning it as an answer to a Question which <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> propounded to our Lord; but the circumstances of both relations are so different, that I cannot think them the same, but do believe these Words spoken at another time. This Doctrine of the forgiveness of our offending Brother, is pressed upon us in several places in the Gospel, and New <ns0:hi>Testament,</ns0:hi> and that upon the gravest Argu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments imaginable, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 6.15. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 18.35. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 11.25. <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 6.37. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.32. from whence we may justly conclude it a duty of very high concernment for us, both to understand, and to live in the practice of. It signifies <ns0:hi>the laying aside of all thoughts or desire of revenge in our own cause.</ns0:hi> The precept is not exclusive of our duty in seeing the Glory of God avenged upon Murderers, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Nor yet of our seeking a just satisfaction in a legal way, for wrongs done to us, relating to our Limbs or Estate, so far as the Person is able to do it; much less doth it require the making such a one as hath so injured us, our intimate and bosom Friend. That which it requireth is the laying aside all <ns0:hi>Malice,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>desire of Revenge,</ns0:hi> upon our Neighbour in a case wherein our own Name or Honour is concerned, and is fitly joyned to what went before. <ns0:hi>This Malice,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>desire of Revenge,</ns0:hi> being the root of all the mischief that Men voluntarily do one to another, especially of that which they do to the innocent Servants of God.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 And the Apostles said unto the Lord, increase our faith.<ns0:note place="bottom">Tho we be not to seek a Connexion of all those speeches of our Lord, which are recorded by the Evangelists, they sometimes heaping together many of his golden sayings, whithout so much as regard to the order of time when he spake them, or their depen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence each on another; yet h<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> that wisely observes the preceding discourse for charity, will easily observe an excellent Connexion of this verse with the former. No duty required of Men and Women, more grates upon Flesh and Blood, then this of <ns0:hi>forgiv<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing injuries,</ns0:hi> nothing that the most of People find harder to put in practice: so as indeed where there is not a root of Faith, this Fruit will not be found. It is Faith which <ns0:hi>worketh by love.</ns0:hi> Till the Soul cometh steadily and fixedly, to agree to those propo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sitions of the Word, where this is required, as the indispensible Will of God. Nay till it comes firmly to rest upon those pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mises and hope for them, which are made to this duty, finally till it comes to have received Christ, and forgiveness from him, and considers it self bound to forgive, as God for Christs sake hath for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />given it, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.32. it will hardly come up to the practice of this du<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty. Hence it is that unregenerate Men, ar<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> usually implacable, Malici<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous, always <ns0:hi>studing Revenge.</ns0:hi> Nay so imperfect are the habits and workings of Faith in Believers, that they often find it very diffi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cult to forgive. The Apostles therefore very properly pray, <ns0:hi>Lord increase our Faith,</ns0:hi> after hearing this discourse; others make the Connexion thus, Lord we have now heard thee discoursing our duty as to Love, <ns0:hi>now increase our Faith,</ns0:hi> discourse to us some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing for the increase of that. But the former seemeth to be <ns0:hi>least</ns0:hi> strained. By the way we may observe from hence, <ns0:hi>that as the beginnings, so the increase of our Faith must be from God.</ns0:hi> In things truly, and spiritually good, <ns0:hi>without</ns0:hi> him we can do nothing.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And the Lord said, If ye had faith as a grain of mustard-seed, ye might say unto this sycamine-tree, Be thou plucked up by the roots, and be thou planted in the sea; and it should obey you.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> hath <ns0:hi>in Effect</ns0:hi> the same <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 17.20. tho he saith <ns0:hi>you might say unto this Mountain.</ns0:hi> See the Notes there I cannot be of their Mind who think that our Saviour in this, and the Parallel place, speaks only of a <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> that work<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:hi>Miraculous Operations.</ns0:hi> The object of which must be a Divine <ns0:hi>Revelation</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Promise</ns0:hi> made to particular Persons, that they shall be able to do things (by the Power of God) out of, and beyond the ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary course of Nature. I do believe that in both Texts our Lord de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />signs, to shew the great honour he will give to the exercise of the Grace of Faith. So as nothing which shall be for the honour of God, and the good of those that exercise it, and which God hath promised shall be too hard, or great an atchievment for it; yet will it not thence follow, that if we <ns0:hi>had Faith,</ns0:hi> that is a <ns0:hi>full persuasion,</ns0:hi> that God would do such a thing by us, and a rest and confidence in God relating to it, we might remove Mountains, or cast Syca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mine-trees into the Sea, for no such Faith in us now could have <ns0:hi>a Promise</ns0:hi> for the object, so as such a Persuasion would be no Faith, but a meer Presumption. But there are other things as difficult, for which all believers have Promises. <ns0:hi>Sin shall have no Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />minion over you. Resist the Devil and he will flee from you,</ns0:hi> &c. and there are duties to be performed by us, as hard in the view of our Natural Eye, as <ns0:hi>removing Mountains,</ns0:hi> amongst which this of forgiving Injuries, is not the least, especially to some Natural tempers. But (saith our Saviour) do not think it impossible to do, you have said well to me, Lord increase our Faith, <ns0:hi>for if you had Faith as a grain of Mustard-seed,</ns0:hi> either so small as a grain of Mustard-seed, (if true) or so <ns0:hi>lively and working,</ns0:hi> that had such a principle of Life in it, as a grain of Mustard-seed, you might do any duty, resist any Temptation, mortifie any Cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ruption, and you that have a Power given you, and a Promise made you for working Miracles, might say to this Sycamine-tree, <ns0:hi>be removed,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:317" />7 But which of you having a servant plowing, or feeding cattel, will say unto him by and by, when he is come from the field, Go, and sit down to meat?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 And will not rather say unto him, Make ready wherewith I may sup, and gird thy self, and serve me till I have eaten and drunken; and afterward thou shalt eat and drink?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 Doth he thank that servant because he did the things that were comanded him? I trow not.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.<ns0:note place="bottom">The 7, 8, 9. verses are plainly a <ns0:hi>Parable,</ns0:hi> a part of a discourse wherein our Lord, under an earthly similitude instructeth us in a spiritual Duty. This Duty is easily learned from the <ns0:hi>Epiparabole, v.</ns0:hi> 10. and it lyeth in two things. 1. <ns0:hi>That we ought to do all those things which our Lord hath commanded us.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>That we, when we have done all, are to look for our reward, not of debt, but of Grace.</ns0:hi> He illustrateth this by a Similitude or Parable. He supposeth a Man to have a Servant, Plowing or feeding Cattel for him. By Servants we must understand, such Servants as they had in those Countries, who were not <ns0:hi>day Servants,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Covenant Servants,</ns0:hi> who are only obliged to work their hours, or according to their Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tracts with us; but such Servants as were most usual amongst them, who were bought with their Money, or <ns0:hi>taken</ns0:hi> in War, who were wholly at their Masters Command, and all their time was their Masters, and they were obliged by their labour only to serve him; such Servants our Lord supposeth to have been abroad in the field, Plowing, or Sowing, or feeding Cattel, and at Night to be come in from their Labour. He asks them which of them would think themselves obliged presently to set them to Supper, (for Meat, Drink, and Clothes, were all such Servants wages) or would not rather set them to work again, to make ready their Masters Supper, and then to wait upon him, tying up their long Garments, which they used in those Countries to wear, promising them, that afterwards also they should Eat and Drink. And sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pose they do that without Murmuring? he asketh them again, whether they would take themselves obliged to thank them, for doing the things which their Master commanded? He tells them he supposeth they would not take themselves to be under any such obligation. Now what is the meaning of all this, he tells them, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11. <ns0:hi>So likewise ye, when you have done all those things which are command you, say, We are unprofitable Servants,</ns0:hi> for the infi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nitely Glorious and Blessed God, can receive no benefit by our services; <ns0:hi>we have done that which was our Duty to do.</ns0:hi> By which we are instructed. 1. <ns0:hi>That we are wholly the Lords,</ns0:hi> all our time, strength, abilities; we are obliged to love the Lord, with all our Heart, and Mind, and Soul, and Strength. 2. That our labour for the Lord must not cease, till the Lord ceaseth commanding; till we have done all that the Lord by his revealed Will lets us know we have to do. 3. That when we have done all, we shall have <ns0:hi>merit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed</ns0:hi> nothing at Gods hands. 1. Because we are Servants. 2. Because we have but done our duty. 4. That the Lord may delay our re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward till we have done all that he hath commanded us. 5. <ns0:hi>That when we have it,</ns0:hi> it is not a <ns0:hi>reward of thanks, but of Grace.</ns0:hi> This Parable is excellently added to the former discourses, our Saviour had before pressed the <ns0:hi>Doctrine of Charity,</ns0:hi> he had also shewed what must be the root of it, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> true and lively Faith, he here sheweth us what we should propose to our selves, as our end in such acts, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> not to merit at the hand of God, not meerly in hope to receive a reward from him, but the <ns0:hi>Glorifying of God,</ns0:hi> by a Faithful obedience to his Will, owning him as our Lord, and our selves as his Servants, without any vain Glory, or Ostentation, and in all Humility, confessing our selves Servants, unprofitable Servants, and such as have but done our Duty, no tho we had done all that he Commanded us, waiting for our reward with patience and taking it at last as of his free Grace with thankfulness, which is indeed requisite to the true and regular performance of eve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry good work which we do, and our Duty if the infirmity of our flesh would allow us to do all whatsoever God hath commanded us; but much more when our performance are so Lame and imperfect, that the greatest part of what we do, amounteth not to the least part of what we leave undone.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 And it came to pass, as he went to Jerusalem, that he passed through the midst of Samaria and Ga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lilee.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And as he entred into a certain village, there met him ten men that were lepers, which stood afar off.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 And they lifted up <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> voices, and said, Jesus Master, have mery on us.<ns0:note place="bottom">Christs nearest way from <ns0:hi>Galilee</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> was through <ns0:hi>Samaria.</ns0:hi> In a certain Town ten Lepers met him, for tho the Law forbad them any other Society; yet it did not restrain them from the Society each of other, probably they were got together, that they might at once come to this great Physician. The Leprosie was a sore Disease, not so much known in our Countries. We shall observe it was the Disease which God made to come upon some Persons, to testifie his displeasure for some Sin committed by them. It was threatned as the Mark of God upon Men for Sin, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28.27. <ns0:hi>from the Scab whereof thou canst not be healed.</ns0:hi> God sent it upon <ns0:hi>Miriam, Num.</ns0:hi> 12.10. for her contempt of <ns0:hi>Moses. David</ns0:hi> curseth <ns0:hi>Ioabs</ns0:hi> house with it 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 3.29. <ns0:hi>Gehazi</ns0:hi> suffereth by it, for his lying and going after <ns0:hi>Naaman</ns0:hi> for a bribe, 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 5.27. King <ns0:hi>Vzziah</ns0:hi> for usurping the Priest's Office, 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 15.5. These ten Lepers cry to Christ for Mercy, Mercy with respect to their Afflictions.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And when he saw <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi>; he said unto them, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Levit. 13.2.</ns0:note> Go shew your selves unto the priests. And it came to pass, that as they went, they were cleans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed.<ns0:note place="bottom">It was according to the Divine Law, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 14.2. That the Leper in the Day of his cleansing, should be brought unto the Priest, who was to judge whether he was healed yea or no, and to offer the offering there prescribed. Christ sends him to the <ns0:hi>Priest,</ns0:hi> partly that he might observe the Law which his Father had given in the case, partly that he might have a testimony of this his Mira<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />culous Operation. We shall observe that our Saviour cured some being at distance from them, some by the Word of his Power only, tho he were present in the same place, others by touching of them; he certainly chose thus to vary his circumstances, in actions of this Nature, to let People know that the healing vertue was inherent in him, and that the proceeding of it from him, was not tyed to any ceremony used at the doing of the Work, which he used or omitted according to his pleasure.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 And one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, and with a loud voice glorified God,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 And fell down on <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> face at his feet, giving him thanks: And he was a Samaritane.<ns0:note place="bottom">It is most probable that this Leper first shewed himself to the Priest, according to the Commandment and the direction of our Saviour, and then returned to give our Saviour thanks. Some think that this <ns0:hi>glorifying</ns0:hi> God here mentioned, and his giving thanks to Christ, signifie the same thing<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> I doubt it, because no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing appeareth from this Story sufficient to convince us, that he looked upon Christ as God; nay it doth not appear that his Faith was risen so high as to believe him, the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> the Son of <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> they speak to him only under the notion of <ns0:hi>Iesus, Master, v.</ns0:hi> 13. It is plain they believed him at least to be a great Prophet, sent from God, and cloathed with a Power from God. I chuse rather therefore to Interprete <ns0:hi>his falling down on his face at his Feet,</ns0:hi> as an humble posture of Reverence, which those Nations did often use to complement their Superiours by, even as a posture of <ns0:hi>Ado<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration,</ns0:hi> and that his <ns0:hi>glorifying God,</ns0:hi> was a praising of him as the principal efficient cause of his healing, and his <ns0:hi>giving thanks</ns0:hi> to Christ, a civil respect paid to Christ as Gods instrument in the case. The <ns0:hi>Evangelist</ns0:hi> addeth, <ns0:hi>and he was a</ns0:hi> Samaritane. Christ calls him a <ns0:hi>Stranger, v.</ns0:hi> 18. A Stranger to the Common-Wealth of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> as all the <ns0:hi>Samaritanes</ns0:hi> were.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And Jesus answering, said, Were there not ten cleansed? but were <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the nine?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 There are not found that returned to give glory to God, save this stranger.<ns0:note place="bottom">These ten Lepers were a representation of all Mankind, not more then one of ten that receive signal Mercies, from the bounti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful hand of Divine Providence, cometh to give God any sutable homage. Thus he maketh his Sun to shine, and his rain to fall upon the Just, and upon the Unjust. Men howl to God upon their beds, but glorifie him not when they are raised up. But this in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crepation of our Saviour lets us know, that this their way is their folly.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 And he <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Math. 9.22. Mark 5.34. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 10.52.</ns0:note> said unto him, Arise, go thy way; thy faith hath made thee whole.<ns0:note place="bottom">It is a wonderful thing to observe what small Rudiments, and Embryoes of Faith, Christ encourageth, and rewardeth. His Faith appeareth to be no more, then a Perswasion that Christ did not do, what things he did of this Nature, by any <ns0:hi>Magical</ns0:hi> Art, (as the <ns0:hi>Pharisee</ns0:hi> blasphemed) but <ns0:hi>by the Power of God,</ns0:hi> and that he was a Man sent of God. This Faith Christ honoureth, commendeth, rewardeth. <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> is to be measured from the <ns0:hi>Revelation,</ns0:hi> which he who believeth hath, and from the <ns0:hi>Opposition</ns0:hi> which he encoun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />treth, a little Faith, upon a little Light, and maintained against a great Opposition is a <ns0:hi>great Faith,</ns0:hi> tho little in it self, yet great with respect to the circumstances of him, or her that be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieveth.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:318" />20 And when he was demanded of the Pharisees, when the kingdom of God should come; he answered them, and said, The kingdom of God cometh not <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>outward shew.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> with observation.<ns0:note place="bottom">Whether the Pharisees spake this deriding him, who in his discourses had been often mentioning a Kingdom of God to come, or in simple seriousness, for they generally expected the coming of a <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> and a secular Kingdom, which he should exercise in the Earth, particularly over the Jews, (having first destroyed the Gentiles) is very hard to determine; their mean opinion of Christ, inclineth some to think the former; their generally re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceived opinion about the Kingdom of the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> giveth some countenance to the latter. Our Saviour's answer fitteth them, whatsoever they intended by their question. <ns0:hi>The Kingdom of God,</ns0:hi> (faith he) <ns0:hi>cometh not <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                           <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> with Obser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation.</ns0:hi> The Word signifies a scrupulous and Superstitious Obser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation. Thus the verb from whence it cometh signifieth, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.10. The verb also signifies a <ns0:hi>captious Observation, Mark</ns0:hi> 3.2. <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 6.7. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 14.1. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 20.20. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 9.24. But that sense cannot agree to the Nown used in this place, the generality of the best Inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />preters agree the sense here to be, <ns0:hi>with external Pomp and Splen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dour,</ns0:hi> and therefore <ns0:hi>Beza</ns0:hi> expounds the Nown here by a <ns0:hi>Peri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phrasis, Ita ut observari poterit,</ns0:hi> in such a manner, as it can be observed. As if he had said. Men have taken up a false Notion of my Kingdom, as if it were to be a secular Kingdom to be set up in the World, with a great deal of Noise and Pomp and Splen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dour. So as Men may observe it and gaze upon its coming. But that which I call my Kingdom is not of this Nature. Our Lord expoundeth it in the next verse. <ns0:hi>The Kingdom of God is within you,</ns0:hi> it is of a spiritual Nature not obvious to humane senses, but exercised over the hearts of my People, whether our Saviour speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth this in reply to the Pharisees, or (as some think) beginning a discourse with his Disciples, which he further pursueth I cannot determine.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Neither shall they say, Lo here, or Lo there: for behold, the kingdom of God is <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>amongst you.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> within you.<ns0:note place="bottom">The latter Words of this verse seem fairly to admit of a double Interpretation, as <ns0:hi>you</ns0:hi> here may signifie the Disciples of Christ, who had received Christ as their Lord, over whom he exercised a spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual Dominion, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>urisdiction, or as it may respect the <ns0:hi>whole Iewish Nation,</ns0:hi> amongst whom the Kingdom of God was now exercised, by the Preaching of the Gospel, and the Power of Christ put forth in the casting out Devils, and other Miraculous Opera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions. I incline to the latter, as differing from those that think these Words were spoken with a peculiar respect to the Disciples, I rather think them a reply to the Pharisees, as corrective of their false Notion, and apprehension of the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> as if he were yet to come, and to set up a temporal principality, for it is said, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. <ns0:hi>And he said unto the Disciples,</ns0:hi> as if he did but then specially apply his discourse to them <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> thus signifieth, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 7.16. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 1.14. you (saith our Saviour) are much mistaken, as to the Nature of my Kingdom, and indeed of the Kingdom of the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> in the expectation of which you live. It is not a King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom of the same Nature with the Kingdoms of the World, it cometh not with Pomp and Splendour for Men and Women to observe; they shall not say, <ns0:hi>Lo here</ns0:hi> he cometh, or <ns0:hi>Lo there</ns0:hi> he goeth, the Kingdom of God is now in the midst among you, tho you observe it not.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 And he said unto the disciples, The days will come when ye shall desire to see one of the days of the Son of man, and ye shall not see <ns0:hi>it.</ns0:hi>
                  <ns0:note place="bottom">Our Lord spendeth his further discourse in this Chapter, in a forewarning of his Disciples of those great troubles, which should follow his departure from them. At present the Bridegroom was with them, and they could not Mourn, for many years after that he was departed from them, <ns0:hi>the days of the Son of Man conti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nued,</ns0:hi> that is Gospel days, times wherein the Gospel of Christ was freely Preached to them. But (saith he) make use of that time, for it will not hold long, there will come a time when you shall desire to see one of the days <ns0:hi>of the Son of Man,</ns0:hi> and shall not see them. These evil days began, when false Christs and false Prophets rose up, which was most eminently a little before the Destruction of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> which happened about forty years after, every Factious Person that had Reputation enough to make himself the head, and leader of a Faction, taking his advan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tage of the common errour of the Jews, that a <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> a Christ was to come, who should exercise a temporal Kingdom over the Jews, would pretend to be, and give out he was the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> to draw a Faction after him. This is that which our Saviour saith in the next Words.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 And they shall say to you, See here, or See there: go not after <ns0:hi>them,</ns0:hi> nor follow <ns0:hi>them.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 For as the lightening that lighteneth out of the one <ns0:hi>part</ns0:hi> under heaven, shineth unto the other <ns0:hi>part</ns0:hi> under heaven: so shall also the Son of man be in his day.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth</ns0:hi> 24.23, 27. You will (saith our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour) have a great many <ns0:hi>false Christs,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>false Prophets</ns0:hi> arise, and foolish credulous People will be deceived by them, and come and tell you, <ns0:hi>Lo</ns0:hi> yonder is the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> or Lo he is in another place, but believe them not. So it is in <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 13.21. <ns0:hi>follow them not,</ns0:hi> saith <ns0:hi>Luke.</ns0:hi> The Son of Man shall have <ns0:hi>his Day,</ns0:hi> a Day when he will come in a Glorious manner to Judge the Quick, and the Dead; but it will come upon the World like <ns0:hi>Lightning,</ns0:hi> that suddenly shineth from one part of Heaven to another, so as no Man can foretel it, or observe the Motion of it. Some do think that by the <ns0:hi>Day of the Son of Man,</ns0:hi> here was meant the spreading of his Gospel, but certainly, it is a strained sense, nor was the spreading of that a thing so sudden, but more gradually, and ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />servably accomplished.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 But first <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mark 8.31. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 9.31. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 10.33.</ns0:note> must he suffer many things, and be rejected of this generation.<ns0:note place="bottom">Before my Kingdom shall appear in that Glory, I must suffer many things, and be rejected of this Generation; you may be seduced to think that I am going to put on a Crown as a secular Prince to deliver you from your Enemies. Alas! I am going to a Cross: I shall have <ns0:hi>a day,</ns0:hi> but this is <ns0:hi>mine Enemies Day,</ns0:hi> and the Power of Darkness both with reference to me and you. Look for nothing in, or from this generation but to see mee mocked, scourged, spit upon, buffetted, hanged upon a Cross, rejected, by Men, these will be the issues of Divine Providence, as to this Generation, look for better things hereafter, but look for no better, from, or in this Generation.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 7.</ns0:note> And as it was in the days of Noe, so shall it be also in the days of the Son of man.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 They did eat, they drank, they married wives, they were given in marriage, until the day that Noe entred into the ark: and the floud came and destroyed them all.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 19.</ns0:note> Likewise also as it was in the days of Lot, they did eat, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they builded.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 But the same day that Lot went out of Sodom, it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroy-them all.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 Even thus shall it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 24.37, 38. Our blessed Lord in these Verses doth both declare the surprisal of the Jews, with that Judgment which was coming upon them, and of the World, with his coming in the Day of Judgment (of which the Destruction of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> was a Type) and also forewarneth them to take heed, that they might not be surprized; he tells them, that <ns0:hi>in the Days of the Son of Man.</ns0:hi> (So that he speaketh of more than one Day) the Day of his Power in the Destructi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of the Jews, and in the Day of Judgment, the Antitype to the former, it shall be as in the Days of <ns0:hi>Noe,</ns0:hi> and of <ns0:hi>Lot.</ns0:hi> In the Days of those Men, neither the Men of the old World, nor the Men of <ns0:hi>Sodom</ns0:hi> would hearken either to <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Lot,</ns0:hi> who were Preachers of Righteousness to them, and gave them Exam<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples of Sober, and Holy Lives, but gave up themselves to Luxu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry, and lived in a careless regard of any thing God was doing, until the very Day, that <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> went in the Ark, with his Fami<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, and the Flood destroyed all the rest, and till the Day that <ns0:hi>Lot</ns0:hi> went out of <ns0:hi>Sodom,</ns0:hi> and Fire and Brimstone came down and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroyed all those who were left in <ns0:hi>Sodom.</ns0:hi> So it would be before the Final ruin of the World. Till the very Days came, and Men felt it, the Generality of Men would not believe it, nor make any preparation for it. But in our Lords propounding these two great Examples to them, he also lets them know their Duty, and Wisdom, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> to Watch, and be upon their Guard, with <ns0:hi>Lot</ns0:hi> to get ready to go out of <ns0:hi>Sodom,</ns0:hi> with <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> to prepare an Ark upon this Admonition which he gave them. There are no such Signs of approaching ruin to Persons or Nations, as <ns0:hi>Security,</ns0:hi> and the abounding of Sin and Wickedness; notwithstanding the warn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings which God giveth them by his Messengers.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 In that day, he which shall be upon the house-top, and his stuff in his house, let him not come down to take it away: and he that is in the field, let him likewise not return back.<ns0:note place="bottom">These Words seem to relate singly to the <ns0:hi>Destruction of Ieru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />salem.</ns0:hi> We had the same, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 24.17, 18. See the <ns0:hi>Notes</ns0:hi> there. They only signify the certain Ruin and Destruction of the place. and are our Saviours Counsel to his Disciples, not to linger, or promise themselves any longer security there, notwith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing what any <ns0:hi>false Christs,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>false Prophets</ns0:hi> should plain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly tell them, but to make as much hast away out of it, as they possibly could.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 Remember Lots wife.<ns0:note place="bottom">We have the Story, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 19.26. <ns0:hi>She looked back from be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hind him, and she became a Pillar of Salt. Lot</ns0:hi> and his Family leaving <ns0:hi>Sodom,</ns0:hi> either looked back, as not believing what the An<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gel had said, or as moved with the miserable condition of the place, or as loth to leave her Estate, and Goods; however in dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />obedience to the command of God, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 17. <ns0:hi>Escape for thy Life look not back neither stay thou in all the plain, escape to the Moun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain; lest thou be consumed.</ns0:hi> God turneth her <ns0:hi>into a Pillar of Salt.</ns0:hi> It is a dreadful caution, against <ns0:hi>unbelief, disobedience, worldly mindedness, Contempt of Gods threatnings, and keeping a love for the forbidden Society of lewd and wicked Persons.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:318" />33 Whosoever shall seek to save his life, shall lose it,<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and whosoever shall lose his life, shall pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serve it.<ns0:note place="bottom">That is, whosoever in disobedience to my command shall use Arts to preserve his Life, shall lose it, and whosoever at my com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand shall be ready to lose it, shall preserve it, or if he loseth his <ns0:hi>Breath,</ns0:hi> he shall preserve his Soul. See the <ns0:hi>Notes</ns0:hi> on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 10.39. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 16.25. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 8.35.</ns0:note>
